stations.title: Assess this hepatomegaly and give your differential
stations.task: This patient has a liver edge palpable on routine examination. Confirm true hepatomegaly, characterise it, and present a differential in six minutes.
examinerQuestions: How did you confirm this is true hepatomegaly rather than a liver pushed down?
Describe the margin, surface and consistency you found, and what each suggests.
Is this liver tender? What does that single fact do to your differential?

skill.exam.gi.liver_cause.title: Reading the cause from margin, surface and consistency
skill.exam.gi.liver_cause.oneLine: Four characteristics, examined in order, turn a palpable edge into a differential
skill.exam.gi.liver_cause.why: Span alone confirms hepatomegaly. What actually narrows the cause is margin, surface, consistency and tenderness, examined and described as a deliberate set every time, not noted only when obviously abnormal.
skill.exam.gi.liver_cause.body: Once hepatomegaly is confirmed by span, describe the edge, margin, surface, consistency, tenderness and pulsatility as a fixed set, since together they are what point towards a cause.
pitfalls: Reporting only 'liver enlarged, span 16 cm' without describing margin, surface or consistency.
Missing pulsatility, a genuine and examinable finding, because it was not deliberately tested for.
Assuming any nodular liver is cirrhosis rather than considering metastatic disease.

probes.q: What does a nodular liver surface suggest?
Distinguish the causes of a rounded versus a sharp hepatic margin.
probes.a: Rounded suggests infiltrative disease; sharp suggests metastases, hepatitis, or biliary obstruction.

probes.q: A liver is firm to hard, non-tender, with a nodular surface and a normal span-to-edge relationship is not applicable since the span itself is markedly increased at 14 cm. What is the leading concern?
probes.a: Hepatoma (hepatocellular carcinoma) or metastatic malignancy, given the firm nodular painless enlargement with a substantially increased span.

keyPoints: Rounded margin: infiltrative disease. Sharp margin: metastases, hepatitis (acute or chronic), or biliary obstruction.

Smooth surface: malaria, acute hepatitis, infiltrative disease. Nodular surface: metastatic cancer, hepatoma, or cirrhosis (classically micronodular in alcoholic disease, macronodular after hepatitis).
Firm-to-hard consistency: metastatic cancer and obstructive jaundice. A soft liver is typical of fatty change, early hepatitis, or congestion.
Tender: right heart failure, acute hepatitis, liver abscess, hepatoma, hepatic infarcts, acute Budd-Chiari syndrome. Painless: fatty liver, infiltrative disease, malaria, leukaemia, lymphoma.
Pulsatile: tricuspid regurgitation (systolic pulsation) or tricuspid stenosis (diastolic), and also described in hepatocellular carcinoma and haemangioma.
Massive hepatomegaly (over 10 cm below the costal margin, or a very large span) is a specific pattern most associated with hepatoma.
A palpable, hard, irregular Sister Mary Joseph node at the umbilicus alongside hepatomegaly should raise metastatic gastric, pancreatic or ovarian malignancy.

skill.hepatomegaly.differential.title: Differential diagnosis of hepatomegaly
skill.hepatomegaly.differential.oneLine: Five headings cover almost every cause: infections, malignancy, infiltration, blood, and vessels
skill.hepatomegaly.differential.why: Causes of hepatomegaly are conventionally grouped under five headings, and learning the headings, not just the examples, is what lets you generate a reasonable differential for a cause you have not specifically memorised.
skill.hepatomegaly.differential.body: Group the differential under five headings: infections, malignancies, infiltrative disorders, haematological disorders, and vascular disorders.
pitfalls: Listing individual diseases without the organising headings, making the differential hard to generate under pressure.
Forgetting the vascular category (heart failure, Budd-Chiari) when the liver findings do not fit an obviously hepatic disease.
Not naming malaria or kala-azar in an endemic setting.

probes.q: Name the five headings under which causes of hepatomegaly are conventionally grouped.
probes.a: Infections, malignancies, infiltrative disorders, haematological disorders, and vascular disorders.

probes.q: Give two vascular causes of hepatomegaly.
probes.a: Right heart failure (or constrictive pericarditis) and Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein obstruction); veno-occlusive disease is also accepted.

probes.q: A patient has hepatomegaly with a raised JVP, bibasal crackles, and pedal oedema. Which of the five headings does this belong to, and name the mechanism.
probes.a: Vascular: congestive hepatomegaly from right heart failure, where a raised systemic venous pressure is transmitted back through the hepatic veins and engorges the liver.

rubric.text: Organises the differential under the five standard headings

keyPoints: Infections: viral hepatitis (acute and chronic), amoebic or pyogenic liver abscess, malaria, kala-azar, tuberculosis, hydatid disease.
Malignancies: hepatocellular carcinoma (hepatoma), metastatic disease (commonly from GI, breast, lung primaries), and, involving the liver secondarily, lymphoma and leukaemia.
Infiltrative disorders: fatty liver (alcoholic or non-alcoholic), amyloidosis, glycogen storage disease, and other storage disorders.
Haematological disorders: chronic haemolytic anaemia, myeloproliferative disease, leukaemia, lymphoma.
Vascular disorders: right heart failure and constrictive pericarditis (congestive hepatomegaly), Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein obstruction), and veno-occlusive disease.
The tender/painless split and the margin-surface-consistency findings from examination are what select the leading heading, rather than working through all five equally in every patient.

skill.ix.hepatomegaly.workup.title: Working up hepatomegaly
skill.ix.hepatomegaly.workup.oneLine: Liver function tests give the pattern; imaging gives the shape and the mass
skill.ix.hepatomegaly.workup.why: Liver function tests are ordered as a panel, but read as a PATTERN: which values are raised, and by how much relative to each other, points towards hepatocellular, cholestatic, or infiltrative disease before imaging is even done.
skill.ix.hepatomegaly.workup.body: Read the liver function tests as a pattern first, then image, then direct further tests by the leading category.
pitfalls: Ordering liver function tests without interpreting the RATIO between transaminases and alkaline phosphatase, which is where the actual pattern lives.
Skipping alpha-fetoprotein in a cirrhotic patient with new or changing hepatomegaly.
Treating a normal ultrasound as excluding all hepatobiliary pathology in a patient with a strong clinical suspicion; a repeat or a different modality may still be needed.

probes.q: Distinguish a hepatocellular from a cholestatic liver function test pattern.
probes.a: Hepatocellular: AST/ALT disproportionately raised relative to alkaline phosphatase. Cholestatic: alkaline phosphatase (and gamma-GT) disproportionately raised relative to the transaminases.

probes.q: Which tumour marker is checked when hepatoma is suspected, particularly in a cirrhotic patient?
What does ultrasound add over liver function tests alone in the hepatomegaly workup?
probes.a: It confirms the enlargement objectively, characterises the echotexture (fatty, nodular, or a focal lesion), and screens the biliary tree for dilation, none of which a blood test alone can show.

keyPoints: Hepatocellular pattern: AST and ALT disproportionately raised relative to alkaline phosphatase, as in hepatitis.
Cholestatic pattern: alkaline phosphatase (and gamma-GT) disproportionately raised relative to the transaminases, as in obstructive jaundice or infiltrative disease.
Synthetic function: albumin and prothrombin time, which reflect chronic severity rather than the acute pattern.
Ultrasound abdomen: confirms the enlargement, assesses echotexture (fatty, nodular, or a focal lesion), and screens the biliary tree for dilation.
Alpha-fetoprotein where hepatoma is suspected, particularly with a background of cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B.
Viral hepatitis serology where an infective hepatocellular pattern is found.
A peripheral smear and malaria/kala-azar testing where fever and travel history point that way.
CT or MRI, and biopsy, where ultrasound finds a focal lesion needing further characterisation.
